questions.q: Why does testing 1,000 random, truly skill-free trading strategies against historical data tend to produce a few strategies with impressively high Sharpe ratios?
options: Because markets secretly reward random strategies
Because Sharpe ratio always increases with the number of strategies tested
Because historical data always favors momentum strategies
Pure chance across many trials -- the same reason flipping 1,000 coins produces a few runs of ten heads in a row
questions.explain: This is multiple testing / data dredging: with enough independent trials, some will look great purely by chance, even with zero real predictive skill.

options: A regularization technique for linear models
Using information in a backtest that would not actually have been available at that point in time
Using too few historical data points
Testing a strategy only on assets that still exist today
questions.explain: Look-ahead bias means a backtest accidentally uses data that was not actually knowable at that historical point, such as restated earnings or current index membership applied to the past.

questions.q: What is survivorship bias in a backtest?
options: Testing a strategy only on companies, funds, or assets that still exist today, excluding failures and delistings
Only training on the most recent year of data
Using an overly complex model
Running the backtest multiple times with different random seeds
questions.explain: Survivorship bias flatters results because it silently excludes the assets that failed or were delisted -- often the ones most likely to have exposed a strategy's real weakness.

questions.q: What does the deflated Sharpe ratio (previewed here, covered in Chapter 4) adjust for?
options: Currency exchange rate risk
The age of the historical data
The number of trials or variations tried before finding the reported strategy
Transaction costs only
questions.explain: The deflated Sharpe ratio discounts a strategy's apparent skill based on how many variations were searched to find it, correcting for multiple-testing luck.

questions.q: Why is overfitting an especially acute risk in quantitative finance compared to many other ML applications?
options: Because backtesting is cheap and fast, making it easy to try thousands of variants, combined with naturally low signal and subtle biases that are easy to miss
Because regulators require overfitting
Because financial data is always clean and well-labeled
Because financial models are always deep neural networks
questions.explain: Cheap, repeated backtesting combined with low signal-to-noise and easy-to-miss biases like look-ahead and survivorship bias make it unusually easy to mistake noise for a real edge.
